item.title: Trajectory-Dependent Decoherence and Leakage During Shuttling of Multi-Spin Qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Parallel shuttling minimizes decoherence and leakage at short shuttling distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms it over long distances across 2-, 3-, and 4-spin encodings; multi-spin fidelity loss and leakage decompose analytically into sums of at most seven pairwise spin error parameters ϵjkP.

Grade 0.478 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Yu-Ning Zhang, Aleksandr S. Mokeev, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, David P. DiVincenzo, Viatcheslav V. Dobrovitski

Figure

Average fidelity loss 1−FXO of a 3-spin exchange-only qubit versus dimensionless shuttling length λ for sequential, parallel, and triangular protocols across channel separations δ=0.3,0.6,0.8. Parallel shuttling yields lower error at short range, whereas sequential shuttling wins at long range.

Asks

How do spatial and temporal correlations in magnetic noise affect dephasing and leakage during the shuttling of multi-spin logical qubits across different trajectories?

But

Pure dephasing via rotating-frame secular Hamiltonian (neglecting x,y noise and spin relaxation). Neglects inter-spin exchange interaction during shuttling. Assumes stationary, isotropic Gaussian noise field.

Tools

Gaussian random field model of spatio-temporal 1/f noise · mixed-unitary dephasing quantum channel · pairwise dephasing factor expansion · Pauli transfer matrix analysis

Abstract

Logical qubits encoded in collective states of multiple spins are promising building blocks for large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. As novel fault-tolerant architectures increasingly rely on qubit shuttling, understanding decoherence of the shuttled multi-spin qubits becomes crucial. We analyze fidelity and leakage of the logical qubits dephased by the spatio-temporally correlated 1/f noise, considering two-, three-, and four-spin encodings. We study different shuttling protocols and establish that for all encodings generally, parallel shuttling provides the best protection against decoherence at short distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms others for long-range transport (although the exact boundaries depend on the specific device parameters). We explain this common behavior in terms of the dephasing factors of pairs of the shuttled spins; we provide explicit expressions for fidelities and leakage, thus enabling experimentalists to predict performance of the multi-spin qubits from only several independently measured pairwise dephasing factors. Our results establish a connection between shuttling trajectories, noise correlations, and qubit decoherence, and provide guidance for achieving noise-resilient shuttling in scalable semiconductor quantum processors.

item.title: Quantum Interference Control of Coupled Atomic Spins
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Non-resonant LZSM interferometry driven by STM bias voltage achieves coherent remote spin flips of a Ti atom coupled to Fe with 97.3% to 99.3% inversion probability in 14.2 ns to 19.8 ns, leaving the Ti spin directly under the tip unchanged.

Grade 0.469 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Sergio Santiago Gomez, Gustavo Mauricio Meneses Ancalle, Daniel Domínguez, María José Sánchez, Alejandro Ferrón

Figure

Remote Ti spin-flip transition probability versus time (top panels) and versus dc and rf driving voltages at ωt=3π (bottom panels), showing selective population inversion exceeding 97% on nanosecond timescales.

Asks

Can quantum interference from non-resonant driving flip a remote atomic spin while protecting it from STM tunneling-electron decoherence?

But

Numerical simulation assuming fast-driving regime δ≪1; Ti-Ti-Fe trimer on MgO/Ag; neglects dipolar coupling relative to exchange; does not simulate explicit dissipation or bath dynamics.

Tools

effective spin Hamiltonian · exact diagonalization · LZSM interferometry · STM bias-voltage driving

Abstract

We propose a protocol for the non-resonant electric control of quantum states in atomic-scale spin systems using Landau-Zener-Stückelberg-Majorana (LZSM) interferometry. We focus on a Ti-Ti-Fe trimer on a thin MgO layer, a platform that has recently emerged as a promising candidate for qubit realization using electron spin resonance combined with scanning tunneling microscopy (ESR-STM). We first analyze a Ti dimer in the absence of the Fe atom and show, through a detailed spectroscopic study, that avoided level crossings can be engineered by combining the in-plane component of the external magnetic field, the tip magnetic field, and the applied bias voltage, which allows the system to be tuned electrically through these crossings. Based on this, we develop LZSM protocols for coherent state control in the dimer using non-resonant LZSM-STM. We then consider the full trimer, where the Fe atom generates a local magnetic field at the remote Ti atom, enabling non-local spin control. We show that this remote and non-resonant manipulation reduces unwanted effects associated with tunneling electrons and enables quantum operations on short timescales. Our results show that quantum interference can be used as a resource for electrically driven, non-resonant, and non-local spin control in atomic-scale systems. This approach enables fast quantum operations while mitigating decoherence, offering a promising route toward scalable atom-based qubit architectures.

item.title: Parametric CZ Gates in a Tunable Tripod Architecture with Fixed-Frequency Superconducting Qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Simulated parametric-resonance CZ gates across three pairs of fixed-frequency transmon qubits sharing one tunable coupler achieve target-subspace fidelities of 0.9943 (CZ01), 0.9834 (CZ02), and 0.9907 (CZ12). A spectator qubit initially in state |1⟩ suffers significant population distortion, transferring population or leaving the computational space.

Grade 0.468 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Chanpyo Kim, Hansol Kim, Jeongsoo Kang, Younghun Kwon

Figure

Population evolution of states |0110⟩, |0020⟩, and |0200⟩ over 500 ns under modulated coupler flux, demonstrating the parametric resonant interaction between |0110⟩ and |0020⟩.

Asks

Can selective parametric-resonance CZ gates be implemented between all pairs of fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler using only coupler flux modulation?

But

Numerical simulation only, with three energy levels per component and no decoherence, relaxation, dephasing, or flux noise modeled; target fidelities evaluated only on the four-state subspace where the spectator qubit and coupler remain in |0⟩.

Tools

three-level transmon Hamiltonian simulation · time-dependent flux pulse optimization · virtual Z phase correction

Abstract

Efficient implementation of the operations required for quantum error correction in superconducting quantum computers requires high gate fidelity, adequate qubit connectivity, and selective control of interactions. Sharing a single coupler among multiple qubits can improve connectivity, but also requires accounting for its effects on qubits outside the target pair. In this work, we numerically investigate the feasibility of implementing parametric-resonance CZ gates in a tunable tripod structure consisting of three fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler. We modulate the external flux applied to the coupler and optimize the pulse parameters for each qubit pair to construct CZ₀₁, CZ₀₂, and CZ₁₂ gates. We calculate the time evolution of a Hamiltonian that includes three energy levels for each circuit element and evaluate gate fidelity and leakage after virtual Z correction. The fidelities obtained for the target-pair computational blocks, whose input and output basis states have both the coupler and spectator qubit in their ground states, are 0.9943, 0.9834, and 0.9907, respectively. We also find that population preservation at the end of the gate depends on the initial state of the spectator qubit. These results demonstrate the possibility of constructing CZ operations for each qubit pair through flux modulation of a shared coupler while maintaining fixed data-qubit frequencies. They also highlight the need to evaluate performance and optimize control over the full computational space, including the spectator qubit.

item.title: Growth and fabrication of advanced PbTe-Pb quantum devices
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Realized continuous superconducting Pb films extending seamlessly from selective-area-grown PbTe nanowires onto the CdTe substrate with an atomically sharp, in situ-equivalent interface. Thermal annealing at 340 ∘ C cleanly desorbs a sacrificial protective Te capping layer following ex situ dielectric mask removal.

Grade 0.437 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Zehao Yu, Wenyu Song, Lining Yang, Zeyu Yan, Yuhao Wang, Weizhao Wang, Xinchen He, Ruidong Li, Jiaye Xu, Shuai Yang, Zonglin Li, Shan Zhang, Xiao Feng, Tiantian Wang, Yunyi Zang, Lin Li, Runan Shang, Qi-Kun Xue, Ke He, Hao Zhang

Figure

Electron microscopy and step schematics showing sacrificial Te capping, mask removal, shadow wall definition, Te thermal desorption, and deposition of a structurally continuous Pb film with an atomically sharp PbTe-Pb interface.

Asks

How can a continuous superconducting film be deposited across a PbTe nanowire and the substrate without introducing disorder from the dielectric mask?

But

Ultrasonic mask peel-off relies on convergence with auxiliary segmented lines over CdTe undercut regions; Te layer removal requires a short Ar treatment followed by 60 min annealing at 340 ∘ C.

Tools

molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) · Te sacrificial protection layer · ultrasonic mask lift-off · thermal annealing · transmission electron microscopy (STEM)

Abstract

We report recent progress in the growth and fabrication of advanced PbTe-Pb Majorana devices for three-terminal correlation experiments. A critical prerequisite for these devices is a continuous Pb film spanning from the PbTe nanowire to the substrate. In previous studies, PbTe nanowires were spatially separated from the substrate mask, making them unable to fulfill this requirement. To address this issue, we have developed a new growth and fabrication approach. Key fabrication steps are introduced between the PbTe growth and Pb deposition. The top facet of the PbTe nanowire is covered with a Te capping layer before breaking the ultra-high vacuum, enabling ex situ processing for subsequent steps. The mask is then removed, followed by the fabrication of shadow walls. After reloading the chip into the growth chamber, the Te protection layer is removed through thermal decomposition, and the Pb film is subsequently deposited. Notably, a pristine PbTe-Pb interface with an in-situ-equivalent quality can be achieved despite the ex-situ processing. Our technique facilitates the develop of advanced PbTe-Pb quantum devices with complex designs, paving the way toward the realization of topological qubits.

item.title: Scanning Probe Control, Quantum Dynamics, and Dispersive Readout of Suspended Carbon Nanotube Resonators
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Establishes a quantitative hierarchy of rates enabling local AFM-tip driving of a suspended carbon nanotube coupled dispersively to a Cooper-pair box for phonon-parity mapping and quantum-capacitance readout. At 10 mK, baseline thermal phonon occupations are 3.38 for a 54 MHz mode, 0.53 for a 221 MHz mode, and near the ground state for a 5.37 GHz mode.

Grade 0.424 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity quantum electrodynamics for superconducting electrical circuits: An arch…” · Cristian Staii

Figure

Thermal phonon occupation at 10 mK across mechanical frequencies alongside final occupation after resolved-sideband cooling for 54 MHz, 221 MHz, and 5.37 GHz modes.

Asks

How large can a resonant driving force applied by an atomic force microscope tip be before static softening, frequency fluctuations, dephasing, and heating overwhelm coherent control of a suspended carbon nanotube resonator?

But

Single-mode Duffing model neglecting higher flexural modes and internal resonances; rotating-wave approximation for weak Kerr anharmonicity; linearized resolved-sideband cooling model.

Tools

Duffing and Kerr nonlinear quantization · capacitively coupled Cooper-pair box (CPB) · dispersive Jaynes-Cummings mapping · Ramsey interferometry · quantum-capacitance readout

Abstract

Suspended carbon nanotubes (CNTs) offer promising opportunities for quantum nanomechanics owing to their small effective mass, strong electrostatic tunability, and mechanical nonlinearity. We develop a unified theoretical framework for coherent control and readout of a suspended CNT driven by an atomic force microscope (AFM) tip and capacitively coupled to a Cooper-pair box (CPB). We first derive the linear and nonlinear Duffing response of the CNT and quantify the effects of AFM force gradients, tip-position fluctuations, and voltage noise on mechanical stability, dephasing, and heating. These results establish operating conditions for coherent actuation with limited backaction. We then quantize the Duffing oscillator, derive its Kerr anharmonicity, and identify the requirements for selective control of individual vibrational transitions. Estimates of thermal occupation and active cooling illustrate the constraints for CNT modes spanning frequencies from 54 MHz to 5.37 GHz. Finally, we derive the CNT--CPB interaction and its dispersive limit, showing how phonon number and parity can be mapped onto the CPB through Ramsey interferometry and detected using quantum-capacitance readout. The resulting framework identifies the conditions under which localized AFM actuation, nonlinear quantum dynamics, and superconducting state-resolved detection can operate within a single CNT device.

item.title: Strong phonon-coupled trion emission in Janus homobilayer
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Symmetric bilayer WSeS with S/S stacking yields dominant trion emission at cryogenic temperatures and high thermal stability, driven by electron-phonon coupling strength of 3.9 resonant with optical phonon A12 energy of 51 meV.

Grade 0.415 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Tianyishan Sun, Dingkun Bi, Haonan Wang, Hiroto Ogura, Yanlin Gao, Mina Maruyama, Susumu Okada, Shiro Entani, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Kazunari Matsuda, Toshiaki Kato

Asks

Can tailoring interfacial architecture and built-in dipoles in Janus homobilayers achieve thermally robust trion emission via strong electron-phonon coupling?

But

Specific to symmetric S/S stacking configuration with inward-pointing antiparallel built-in electric fields.

Tools

Janus WSeS homobilayer (S/S stacking) · photoluminescence spectroscopy · phonon resonance analysis

Abstract

Janus transition metal dichalcogenides with broken mirror symmetry provide a novel platform for exploring many-body effects mediated by spin-valley-phonon interactions. Strong electron-phonon coupling demands a precise match between a strong effective dipole moment and nanometer-scale charge confinement. Here, we report thermally robust and enhanced trion emission in a symmetric bilayer WSeS with an S/S stacking configuration. The inward-pointing antiparallel built-in electric fields induce a strong electron confinement effect at the interface, driving dominant trion emission at cryogenic temperatures. Furthermore, a massive electron-phonon coupling strength (3.9) resonant with the optical phonon A_1^2 energy (51 meV) contributes to the thermal stability of this trion emission at elevated temperatures. By tailoring the interfacial architecture in Janus WSeS homobilayers, this study overcomes the thermal decoherence limits inherent to traditional semiconductor systems, offering novel insights into room-temperature many-body interactions.

By tailoring the interfacial architecture in Janus WSeS homobilayers, this study overcomes the thermal decoherence limits inherent to traditional semiconductor systems, offering novel insights into room-temperature many-body interactions.

item.title: Exciton design via topological spin textures
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Emergent flux of a magnetic skyrmion transfers to an exciton as a full flux quantum ±ν only when exchange coupling exceeds the spin-orbit threshold J∗=|ΔBD|/2 (or Δc), vanishing completely below it.

Grade 0.411 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Karim Rezouali, Selcuk Sözeri, Samir Lounis

Figure

Emergent flux Φ/Φ0 and scattering properties as a function of the exchange-to-splitting ratio Jc/ΔBD for K and K′ valleys, demonstrating the threshold switch to quantized flux and agreement with exact scattering calculations.

Asks

How do composite neutral excitons with constituent-dependent spin-orbit coupling perceive and interact with topological magnetic spin textures?

But

Projected description holds in adiabatic regime (Ji>ℏ2/(2miw2) and Ji≠Δi); two-dimensional semiconductor assumption; low temperature (4.2 K).

Tools

Two-body adiabatic gauge-field projection · Two-channel scattering theory · Finite-volume radial Schrödinger solver · GW-BSE calculations

Abstract

Excitons carry energy and information through a semiconductor without carrying charge. This makes them attractive for optoelectronics, but also hard to guide. Magnetic skyrmions, on the other hand, are moved by small electrical currents. Here we develop a theory of excitons interacting with a skyrmion in which the electron and the hole are treated as distinct constituents, each with its own spin--orbit coupling. We find that the topology of the skyrmion is transferred to the exciton only when the exchange coupling exceeds the relevant spin--orbit splitting. The exciton then experiences a full flux quantum, with opposite signs in the two valleys. The quantum metric of the spin texture creates a ring-shaped barrier that traps excitons, whereas the topological charge fixes the angular momentum of the trapped states and hence their optical selection rules. Because the trap moves with the skyrmion, excitons can be transported by current pulses, and small skyrmions accommodate a single exciton, which opens the door for potential hybrid applications in future information technology intertwining topological magnetic bits with optical excitations.

item.title: Interaction-enabled charging and thermal crossover of the spin-work deficit in a Hubbard double quantum dot
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Additional work deficit from total spin conservation in a charged Hubbard double quantum dot vanishes above a thermal crossover at s2=q, occurring at kBTc/t0≃0.11607 for detuning-noise amplitude σϵ/t0=0.10.

Grade 0.396 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “exchange gates and two-qubit operations in semiconductor double quantum dots” · Khalil Loukhssami, Cheng Shang, Morad El Baz, Khadija El Hawary

Figure

Spin-work deficit 𝒢ST/t0=(𝒲U(1)−𝒲N,S)/t0 plotted against preparation temperature kBT/t0 and noise amplitude σϵ/t0, showing the boundary where the spin-conservation constraint becomes nonbinding.

Asks

How does spin conservation limit the extractable work of an interacting Hubbard double quantum dot charged in the presence of quasistatic detuning fluctuations?

But

Quasistatic Gaussian detuning disorder only (no 1/f time-resolved noise). Neglects higher orbitals, spin-orbit coupling, phonons, and finite pulse discharge protocols. Direct one-photon transition at representative parameters corresponds to 0.48 THz barrier modulation.

Tools

Extended Fermi-Hubbard model · Passive spectral rearrangement / passivity theory · Gauss-Hermite quadrature averaging · Unitary midpoint time-evolution

Abstract

We study how conservation of total spin affects the extractable work of an interacting Hubbard double quantum dot charged in the presence of unresolved quasistatic detuning fluctuations. The full fermionic Fock space is used to model preparation through electronic reservoirs, whereas the additional work deficit associated with spin conservation arises entirely from the singlet and triplet states at half filling. At zero detuning, modulation of the symmetric tunnel barrier couples two singlets of even parity. The corresponding transition matrix element vanishes when U = V . An exact formula for the additional work deficit follows from passive spectral rearrangement under two extraction constraints: conservation of particle number alone and conservation of both particle number and total spin. At low temperature, an expansion in the detuning response gives a leading estimate of the noise amplitude at which this deficit first appears. Increasing the preparation temperature changes the triplet population and produces a crossover at s2 = q, where the additional spin constraint becomes nonbinding for the averaged state, even though both ergotropies may continue to decrease. We obtain a semi-analytic expression for this crossover by separating the thermal Gibbs weights from the singlet dynamics under a fixed charging pulse. Averaging over symmetric detuning disorder also restores parity in the density matrix and allows singlet eigenvalues of different parity to exchange order, changing the branch that determines the thermal boundary. The work values are optimal over specified classes of unitary operations and do not establish the yield of a finite discharge protocol.
